title: A neural substrate of prediction and reward
why: Dopamine neurons signal reward prediction errors = TD error. The neural root of 'learn from the gap between expected and actual outcome'.

authors: Dabney, Kurth-Nelson, Uchida, Starkweather, Hassabis, Munos, Botvinick
title: A distributional code for value in dopamine-based reinforcement learning
why: Dopamine neurons encode a distribution over outcomes, not a mean: the brain carries uncertainty in its value code. Relevant to calibration / 'knowing what it does not know'.

title: By carrot or by stick: cognitive reinforcement learning in parkinsonism
why: Separate pathways learn from positive vs negative outcomes (dopamine bursts vs dips). Supports separate treatment of success and error signals.

title: The neural basis of human error processing: reinforcement learning, dopamine, and the error-related negativity
why: Anterior cingulate error signal (ERN) is generated when dopamine conveys a negative prediction error; the brain's 'that was wrong' alarm.

title: Conflict monitoring and cognitive control
why: Anterior cingulate monitors conflict between competing responses and recruits more control. A mechanism for 'noticing a contradiction'.

title: Predictive coding in the visual cortex: a functional interpretation of some extra-classical receptive-field effects
why: Feedback carries predictions, feedforward carries residual errors. Origin of the predictive-coding view of cortex.

title: An approximation of the error backpropagation algorithm in a predictive coding network with local Hebbian synaptic plasticity
why: A network using only local Hebbian updates and prediction errors can approximate backprop.

title: Predictive coding approximates backprop along arbitrary computation graphs
why: Predictive coding with local updates matches backprop gradients on arbitrary graphs (CNNs, RNNs, LSTMs).

title: Backpropagation and the brain
why: NGRAD framework: error signals approximated locally by activity differences; backprop-like learning may occur in cortex.

title: Eligibility traces and plasticity on behavioral time scales: experimental support of neoHebbian three-factor learning rules
why: Learning = Hebbian eligibility trace x a third gating factor (reward minus expected, or surprise). The cellular form of 'learn when surprised'.

title: What learning systems do intelligent agents need? Complementary learning systems theory updated
id: Trends in Cognitive Sciences 2016 (DOI not verified)
why: Fast hippocampal episodic learning + slow neocortical structure learning, linked by replay. Blueprint for fast/slow learners.

title: How schema and novelty augment memory formation
why: Schema-congruent info is integrated via prefrontal cortex; schema-incongruent (surprising) info drives hippocampal encoding. How contradictions are stored.

title: Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay
why: Replay order follows expected utility of updating a memory. A principle for which past experiences a learner should rehearse.

title: The Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine: unifying space and relational memory through generalization in the hippocampal formation
why: Separates abstract structure (transition rules, learned slowly, shared across worlds) from content (fast Hebbian bindings). One visit per node suffices in a new world with known structure. Direct support for graph learners and logic transfer.

authors: Behrens, Muller, Whittington, Mark, Baram, Stachenfeld, Kurth-Nelson
title: What is a cognitive map? Organizing knowledge for flexible behavior
why: Map-like relational codes may organise knowledge of all kinds, not just space. Justifies graph state representations.

title: The neural basis of metacognitive ability
why: Metacognitive accuracy is separable from task performance and tied to anterior/lateral prefrontal cortex. Knowing how well you know is a distinct skill.

title: Confidence and certainty: distinct probabilistic quantities for different goals
why: Confidence = probability that a choice is correct (choice-dependent); certainty = posterior precision about a variable. Clean definitions for the H3 confidence head.

title: Neural correlates, computation and behavioural impact of decision confidence
why: Orbitofrontal neurons in rats track decision confidence; confidence drives giving up on a trial (abstention).

authors: Botvinick, Ritter, Wang, Kurth-Nelson, Blundell, Hassabis
title: Reinforcement learning, fast and slow
why: Fast RL = episodic memory + meta-learned inductive biases from a slow outer loop. Explains why a from-scratch learner on 400 puzzles is slow.

authors: Wang, Kurth-Nelson, Kumaran, Tirumala, Soyer, Leibo, Hassabis, Botvinick
title: Prefrontal cortex as a meta-reinforcement learning system
venue: bioRxiv 295964; Nature Neuroscience 2018 (venue not confirmed in my search)
why: Slow dopamine-driven learning sculpts prefrontal dynamics into a second, fast RL algorithm that runs in activations. Direct model for our learning-to-learn experiment.

authors: Wang, Kurth-Nelson, Tirumala, Soyer, Leibo, Munos, Blundell, Kumaran, Botvinick
title: Learning to reinforcement learn
why: Deep meta-RL: a recurrent agent trained by one RL algorithm implements a second, faster one.

authors: Duan, Schulman, Chen, Bartlett, Sutskever, Abbeel
title: RL^2: fast reinforcement learning via slow reinforcement learning
why: Fast RL represented as an RNN whose weights are learned by slow RL; the method our sequence RL follows.

authors: Laskin, Wang, Oh, Parisotto, Spencer, Steigerwald, Strouse, Hansen, Filos, Brooks, Gazeau, Sahni, Singh, Mnih
title: In-context reinforcement learning with algorithm distillation
why: Causal transformer on RL learning histories improves in context. The 'imitate learning histories' control in H1.

title: How to grow a mind: statistics, structure, and abstraction
why: People learn from little data by probabilistic inference over structured, abstract generative models (theories, schemas).

title: Building machines that learn and think like people
why: Machines need causal models, intuitive theories and compositionality with learning-to-learn. Frames what STML should add.

title: Where do hypotheses come from?
venue: CBMM Memo 056 (journal version not confirmed in my search)
why: People sample a few self-generated hypotheses (Monte Carlo) and deviate from rational inference accordingly. A model of human hypothesis revision for Pillar 1.

title: The child as hacker
why: Learning as program improvement: repeated small edits to a symbolic program. Matches the 'local repair' we see in H-ARC revisions.

title: A rational analysis of the selection task as optimal data selection
why: Choosing which test to run = maximizing expected information gain. Basis of the Socratic question q* = argmax information gain.

title: Information-seeking, curiosity, and attention: computational and neural mechanisms
why: Curiosity as information-seeking, computed from learning progress and uncertainty; neural basis.

title: Learning from errors
why: Errorful learning plus corrective feedback helps; high-confidence errors are corrected more (hypercorrection), via surprise and attention to feedback. Core evidence that mistakes teach.

title: Productive failure
why: Attempting problems before instruction, and failing, can improve later learning/transfer (impasse-driven learning). Effect size debated.

title: Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding
why: Prompting learners to explain themselves improves understanding. Basis for the explanation part of the human study. Small sample (N=24).

title: Self-explanations: how students study and use examples in learning to solve problems
why: Good learners generate explanations and monitor understanding better. Correlational.

title: Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention
why: Retrieval practice beats restudy on delayed tests even though restudy feels better. Learning signals and feelings of learning can diverge.

title: Let's verify step by step
why: Process supervision (scoring each reasoning step) beats outcome supervision (final answer only): 78% on a MATH subset. The AI analogue of a Socratic critic that says where the reasoning broke.

title: Solving math word problems with process- and outcome-based feedback
why: Outcome supervision gets similar final-answer error; process-based feedback is needed for correct reasoning (reasoning error 14.0% to 3.4%).

authors: Qi, Xu, Shen, Liu, Jin, Wang, Huang
title: The art of SOCRATIC QUESTIONING: recursive thinking with large language models
why: Recursive self-questioning (ask and answer sub-questions) improves LLM reasoning. Socratic questioning used by the learner itself.

title: Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
why: Agents turn feedback into written reflections stored in memory instead of updating weights (91% pass@1 HumanEval). Learning from mistakes via verbal feedback.

title: Language models (mostly) know what they know
why: Large LMs are well calibrated on multiple-choice/true-false when prompted well and can predict if they know an answer. Prior art for H3 (STML defines 'don't know' as absence of a certificate).

title: Inductive biases for deep learning of higher-level cognition
why: Inductive biases from conscious, sequential, System-2 processing (sparse factors, attention, modularity) for out-of-distribution generalization.

title: Neuroscience-inspired artificial intelligence
why: Survey of how neuroscience has inspired and can keep inspiring AI (memory, attention, planning, transfer).

authors: Piech, Bassen, Huang, Ganguli, Sahami, Guibas, Sohl-Dickstein
title: Deep knowledge tracing
why: RNN models of student knowledge over exercise sequences. Framework for the Duolingo-type log data (single-attempt).

title: On the measure of intelligence
why: Intelligence = skill-acquisition efficiency; introduces ARC. The standard we are measured against.

title: H-ARC: a robust estimate of human performance on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus benchmark
why: Our main human dataset: 1,729 people, 800 tasks, all actions and attempts. 76.2% on training tasks.

title: Confidence as Bayesian probability: from neural origins to behavior
why: Review of confidence as the probability of being correct, its neural origins and behavioural uses. Companion to Pouget et al. 2016.

authors: Anderson, Bothell, Byrne, Douglass, Lebiere, Qin
title: An integrated theory of the mind
why: ACT-R: modules (declarative memory, procedural rules, goal, perception, motor) coordinated by production rules; learning = chunk strengthening with activation + utility learning from reward. A tested human-learning-curve model; a candidate source for the synthetic human learner.

title: A standard model of the mind
why: Proposes a common architecture shared by ACT-R, Soar and others. Useful checklist of components STML lacks (working memory, long-term declarative + procedural memory, learning from reward).

title: SOAR: an architecture for general intelligence
why: Soar: problem solving by search in problem spaces; impasses trigger subgoals; 'chunking' turns resolved impasses into new rules. Impasse-driven learning is the machine version of productive failure / the Socratic question.

title: Reconstructing constructivism: causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms, and the theory theory
why: Children revise intuitive theories through causal Bayesian learning, informal experiments in play, and imitation; theory change from 16 months to 4 years. The developmental version of assimilation / accommodation.

title: Human-level concept learning through probabilistic program induction
why: Concepts as small programs inferred from one example reach human-level one-shot classification and beat deep nets. Evidence for structured priors.

title: People infer recursive visual concepts from just a few examples
why: People infer latent generating programs from 1-3 examples; a Bayesian program-learning model fits, a pretrained deep net does not.

title: Human-like systematic generalization through a meta-learning neural network
why: Meta-learning for compositionality (MLC): train on a changing stream of compositional tasks; only MLC combined systematicity and flexibility among seven models. A meta-learning recipe on a task FAMILY.

title: Statistical learning by 8-month-old infants
why: Infants segment words from a continuous nonsense-syllable stream after ~2 minutes using only transition statistics, with no instruction, reward or feedback. Language structure is learned without explicit error feedback.

title: Early language acquisition: cracking the speech code
why: Infants combine statistical pattern detection with social interaction; social context gates speech learning (Kuhl 2007). Learning signals in language are partly social.

title: Maturational constraints on language learning
why: Learning capacity changes with age: later exposure gives poorer outcomes. A reason to treat 'human learning' as depending on the learner's stage.

title: The cortical organization of speech processing
why: Dual-stream model: a ventral stream maps sound to meaning, a dorsal stream maps sound to articulation. Two coupled pathways for comprehension and production.

title: The brain basis of language processing: from structure to function
why: Syntactic processing relies on left-lateralised temporal and inferior frontal networks; semantic processing on less lateralised temporo-frontal networks.

title: Becoming syntactic
why: A connectionist model that learns syntax by predicting the next word and adjusting on prediction error (my recollection; the search did not confirm the abstract - verify before relying on it).

title: Implicit learning of artificial grammars
venue: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior 6:855-863
why: People classify strings from an artificial finite-state grammar above chance without being able to state the rules. The classic paradigm for an artificial-language version of the game.

title: The memory function of sleep
why: Sleep supports consolidation (offline reactivation). Biological analogue of offline replay in Stage A.

title: A trainable spaced repetition model for language learning
why: Half-life regression on Duolingo data: models forgetting (recall probability decays with time since practice). Retention, not error revision.

title: Second language acquisition modeling
why: Duolingo SLAM shared task: predict future errors of learners from their history (7M+ words, 6k learners in the paper; the call described a smaller set). Word-level errors, one attempt per exercise.
